newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo's Hamanaka faces more legal trouble.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo's Hamanaka faces more legal trouble.

text.p: Former star copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka was indicted on forgery charges Tuesday, while his former employer Sumitomo Corp. accused him of committing fraud in connection with a $2.6 billion trading scandal.

Sumitomo alleged that Hamanaka committed fraud through a newly disclosed Hong Kong connection. Tokyo prosecutors then issued formal indictments against Hamanaka on four counts of forgery. He was arrested three weeks ago.
Under Japanese law, a conviction on the fraud charges would be much more serious than a forgery conviction.

Hamanaka was the most controversial and influential figure in the world copper market until he was fired in June for allegedly racking up $2.6 billion in losses from his apparently unauthorised trades. The losses are the biggest in financial history.
A source close to the Tokyo prosecutors office said Hamanaka would be served with an arrest warrant for fraud on Wednesday, following Sumitomo's filing of the formal fraud complaint.

Hamanaka's arrest on Oct. 22 on suspicion of forgery came one day after Sumitomo filed a complaint with Tokyo prosecutors alleging he forged two documents in 1994 authorising him to engage in certain copper transactions.
Tuesday's indictment included two additional charges that he forged a managing director's name in 1993.
One of Hamanaka's lawyers said the ex-trader could be sentenced for up to 10 years if he is convicted of fraud. A forgery conviction could result in a sentence of up to five years.

Sumitomo has alleged that Hamanaka incurred a loss of 6.5 billion yen ($58 million) from unauthorised trading in 1985, while subsequent secret deals attempting to erase the losses simply compounded them until they snowballed into a multi-billion-dollar catastrophe.
